summary: San Diego sprawls across 373 square miles — larger than the entire footprint of New York City's five boroughs — yet much of that acreage is carved into deep coastal canyons and mesas that fracture the city into dozens of distinct plateaus, giving neighborhoods an almost village-like separation even within a single municipality. That canyon-carved topography means sunset views from surprisingly ordinary streets, but it also means the freeway system (I-5, I-8, I-15, SR-163) functions as connective tissue between mesas, and daily life often orbits highway on-ramps more than sidewalks. The economy is genuinely unusual for a Sun Belt city: military installations and defense contractors sit alongside a major biotech corridor anchored around UC San Diego and Torrey Pines, so switching employers within the same sector rarely requires a ZIP code change. At a median household income of roughly $104,000 and a median home value near $849,000 — an 8.1-to-1 ratio — buying requires either substantial savings or dual incomes, while median rent at $2,223 consumes about 26% of gross household pay, a more manageable threshold. With 9.2 hours of daily sunshine and an average high of 72°F that barely swings ten degrees between seasons, outdoor life is less a weekend event than a default setting — Balboa Park alone offers 1,200 acres of trails, gardens, and museums minutes from downtown. The defining tension is geographic: a city with world-class coastal access and a genuine job base, organized around a landscape that resists the connectedness its size would otherwise demand.
